project.title: Vesuvius Challenge — PHerc0191 First Letters campaign
project.subtitle: Research log: every run, what it asked, what it showed, what changed
project.goal: Find 10 legible letters in a 4 cm² area of an unopened Herculaneum scroll (First Letters, $50k/scroll), and surface evidence-backed tooling fixes along the way (Progress Prizes).
project.scroll: PHerc0191 — 9.362 µm / 113 keV scan 20250821151635, crushed cross-section, full public data (CT, Lasagna normals, tracks, surface predictions). Its clearest band is getting a last, deeper look; PHerc0813 is the next scroll (pilot).
project.hardware: Home: 4-GPU Linux box (2× RTX 3060 12 GB, RTX 3060 Ti 8 GB; GTX 1660 SUPER unusable), i3-9100 4 cores, 1 TB NVMe, 300 Mbps WAN. This is the default. Cloud GPUs (AWS) only when it is cost-effective.
project.fit_chart_note: All fits are band z 9,000–10,000 except the last one, the clear band z 11,200–12,200 (different tracks, so compare with care).

phases.title: Calibrate the ink detector
phases.summary: Prove the render → ink pipeline on a segment with known text before trusting it on new geometry.

phases.title: Pick a scroll and assemble its inputs
phases.summary: PHerc0191: full CT pyramid mirrored (930 GB), Lasagna normals, tracks (9.9 GB), smoothed umbilicus, resident pools.

phases.title: Get geometry that follows the real sheets
phases.summary: Global spiral fit vs. local patch growing. Spiral fits plateau at ~46–49% on-sheet on band z 9,000–10,000; the post-hoc snap + Lasagna flatten (PHerc. 343 recipe) gives windings with clean papyrus weave. On the scroll's clearest band the same recipe reaches 0.519, our best fit with the current fitter.

phases.title: Render + ink at scale
phases.summary: Flatten → render → ink → stroke score → eyes. All 99 flattened windings of band z 9,000–10,000 checked at depths 0 and +1 (7 with four models, 92 with three) plus the community's 10 windings: no ink. Four AWS fleet runs, $22.80 in total, all null; the cloud is now kept for cost-effective jobs and fast deep looks at anything promising.

phases.title: PHerc0191's clearest band
phases.summary: Band z 11,200–12,200, chosen with Scan-Quality-Map: fitted, snapped, 100 windings flattened, rendered and triaged; 7 picked together; four-model deep look at depths −2..+3 (no letters). Next A4: three models on the other 93. Gate A: if the whole band is null, PHerc0191 is set aside (meshes kept).

phases.title: Next scroll: PHerc0813 pilot
phases.summary: Band data downloaded (75 GB). Assemble its spiral dataset, fit one band (z 12,000–13,000), snap, judge the geometry by eye. Gate B: clean geometry → commit to 0813; poor → pilot PHerc0358.

phases.title: The stroke score as a tool
phases.summary: stroke-score 0.1 packaged (MIT). Next: more known-text segments as positives, a measured false-alarm rate on our null windings, release before the Oct 31 Progress Prize deadline.

phases.title: Housekeeping
phases.summary: One data layout, data and code dictionaries, disk cleanup in tiers that wait on the gates, script fixes.

phases.title: Iterate and submit
phases.summary: Depth-offset sweeps where rows appear; document; submit before announcing anything.

experiments.title: Ink detector calibration on PHercParis4 (known text)
experiments.question: Does our render → ink_9um pipeline reproduce readable letters where letters are known to exist?
experiments.technique: vc_render_tifxyz (28 slices, flip-normals) on segment 20231016151002 at 9.6 µm, then ink_9um seeds 42/43, 40k/75k steps, both directions.
experiments.result: Three legible Greek lines in the reverse layer order.
experiments.learned: The ink side works when the geometry is right. Every later null result is a geometry problem until proven otherwise.

experiments.title: PHerc0800 public segments, 36 ink runs
experiments.question: Do the six public PHerc0800 segments contain letters the community missed?
experiments.technique: Same pipeline, 6 segments × 2 seeds × 2 checkpoints × 2 directions.
experiments.result: No letters; mottled noise or blank.
experiments.learned: Re-running public segments is not a shortcut; the prize is in new geometry.

experiments.title: Which eligible scroll? Cross-section survey
experiments.question: Is PHerc0191's crushed cross-section unusual among the eligible 9.36 µm scrolls?
experiments.technique: Level-4 cross-sections at 40% and 65% height for PHerc0125/0211/0813/0826/0257 vs 0191.
experiments.result: All shortlisted scrolls are crushed or folded; 0191 is typical.
experiments.learned: Stay on PHerc0191. Crushed geometry is the norm, so solving it is the whole game.

experiments.title: Pilot spiral fit, z 9000–10000, 10k steps
experiments.question: How well does the minimal-route spiral fit (umbilicus + Lasagna + tracks) follow PHerc0191's sheets?
experiments.technique: spiral-fitting fit_spiral.py, dense_spacing_mode grad_mag, tracks on, no patches/shell/winding model. 46 min on one RTX 3060.
experiments.result: 120 windings exported; on-sheet track points 46%, fully satisfied tracks 8%. Renders of w040/w070/w100 are on-sheet only in patches; ink maps are noise.
experiments.learned: A point counts as on-sheet only within 6 voxels and 0.45 winding of its track's sheet, so more than half the track points are off the fitted surface. Ink is noise until that changes.

experiments.title: Track loss weight ×2
experiments.question: Is the fit under-weighting the track evidence?
experiments.technique: Pilot config with loss_weight_track_radius doubled.
experiments.result: Slightly worse than baseline.
experiments.learned: Weights are not the lever; the model cannot satisfy the tracks as posed.

experiments.title: 30k optimizer steps
experiments.question: Is the fit simply under-converged?
experiments.technique: Pilot config, 3× steps (80 min).
experiments.result: 0.4901 / 0.1018, best of the fits; w040 render: roughly half fibre texture, half laminated crossings — matches the metric.
experiments.learned: Convergence buys three points; it does not move the spiral into the outer third of the papyrus.

experiments.title: Outer shell from the CT mask (sparse) + outer winding 105
experiments.question: Does telling the fitter where the papyrus ends, and how many windings there really are (~100 by ray audit), fix the outer region?
experiments.technique: make_outer_shell.py: boundary of the masked CT every 8 slices → tifxyz; shell_outer_winding_idx 105.
experiments.result: No change — the shell loss was silently zero all run.
experiments.learned: Tooling finding #7: the fitter normalizes shell confidence by its global max; a shell sampled every 8 slices lands every interior value at 0.22, below the 0.25 threshold, so no sample is valid and the loss is 0 with no warning.

experiments.title: Dense outer shell (every slice) + outer winding 105
experiments.question: With the shell loss actually active, does pulling winding 105 to the boundary help?
experiments.technique: Shell regenerated with one row per slice (18,980 rows × 720 bins); otherwise as shell105.
experiments.result: Shell loss active (177 at the end); outer winding moved from 16.5 to 21.5 mm mean radius; track satisfaction dropped.
experiments.learned: Stretching the whole spiral outward hurts the inner tracks: the inner spacing is already about right. The outer, fat sectors need more windings at wider spacing, not a stretched spiral.

experiments.title: Initial winding spacing 16 → 32 voxels
experiments.question: The ray audit's sheet period is 0.25–0.45 mm; does starting the spiral at the real spacing help?
experiments.technique: model_initial_dr_per_winding 32.
experiments.result: Much worse: 93 windings span 32 mm; windings 75+ are mostly in air.
experiments.learned: The spacing is not re-learned by the optimizer: the initial value fixes the spiral's radial extent. The sector-dependent spacing (0.13 mm on the flat sides to 0.26 mm at the ends) needs an anisotropic flow or local supervision, not a global number.

experiments.title: Where the fitted spiral sits vs the papyrus (per 30° sector)
experiments.question: Is the problem spill into air or failure to reach the outer sheets?
experiments.technique: mesh_in_mask.py: per-winding fraction of mesh vertices inside the CT mask; per-sector median radius of the outermost winding vs the CT boundary at z 9525.
experiments.result: No winding is mostly in air. The outermost winding stops 3–8 mm (10–25 sheets) short of the boundary in the fat sectors and only just reaches it in the thin ones.
experiments.learned: A crushed scroll has the same winding count in every direction with spacing varying ~2.5× by sector. The uniform regularizer resists exactly that deformation.

experiments.title: Patch growing (vc_grow_seg_from_seed) without direction fields
experiments.question: Can local patch growing from a seed on a predicted surface avoid the global-spiral problem?
experiments.technique: Empty-space tracing on the surface-prediction volume, 70/150 generations.
experiments.result: Fixed discs of 6.6 / 21–31 cm² regardless of the volume; renders cut across many sheets.
experiments.learned: Without its guidance inputs the tracer ignores the data entirely.

experiments.title: Fiber-direction inference on the band (SD2 model)
experiments.question: Produce the direction field the tracer needs.
experiments.technique: vesuvius fiber_trace_3d.infer, level 0, z 8500–10500, output scaled down 4×; 1.6 h on one 3060 after fixing a missing-module import (tooling finding #8).
experiments.result: nx/ny/presence pyramids. The output is a sheet NORMAL field in Lasagna's compact encoding, not raw fibre directions; the tracer needs an x/y/z layout, so a converter was written.
experiments.learned: Two encodings, one formula ((u8−128)/127), different layouts. Converted with symlinks plus a computed z component.

experiments.title: Patch growing with the Fiber normal field
experiments.question: Does the direction field make the tracer follow a sheet?
experiments.technique: dir: normal, scale 2, presence as confidence weight; 70 and 150 generations.
experiments.result: Still flat discs (6.9 / 21.2 cm²); the field only re-oriented them.
experiments.learned: Every growth candidate was accepted — the data terms were inactive. The docs mark normal grids as REQUIRED for the tracer; no run had passed them.

experiments.title: Patch growing with normal grids + Fiber normal field
experiments.question: With the required normal-grid input, does the patch follow a sheet?
experiments.technique: normal_grid_path (PHerc0191 xy grids, level 0, spiral-step 20) + the direction field; 70 generations, 159 s (4× slower → losses active).
experiments.result: First partly on-sheet patch: large regions of clean fibre texture, one diagonal band still cutting across layers; self-crossing check not clean.
experiments.learned: The patch route is alive. Next: xz/yz normal-grid planes, a cleaner seed, direction weight, Lasagna normals as an alternative field.

experiments.title: Winding-model supervision cache for the band
experiments.question: Give the spiral fitter a local measurement of sheet spacing (the 'winding model') instead of a global number.
experiments.technique: infer_winding_volume.py native-phase cache, bootstrap = exp-30k, winding step 8, seed spacing 96 → 7,102 slabs (~107 GB at 15 MB/slab), then export_spiral_supervision.py; refit with dense_spacing_mode winding_model (exp-wm).
experiments.result: Done: 7,102 slabs, 104 GB, 2 h 47 min on two GPUs (CPU-bound at 1.0–1.4 s/slab). Cache complete; exported (see next entry). exp-wm, the first fit using it, is running.
experiments.learned: The smoke run sized the full cache: the documented (step 3, spacing 60) settings would have needed 776 GB.

experiments.title: Patch growing: direction weight 3, 100 generations, normal grids
experiments.question: Does a stronger direction-field weight remove the sheet crossings?
experiments.technique: As the normal-grid run with direction_fields weight 3.0 and 100 generations (304 s).
experiments.result: 16.9 cm² patch; more on-sheet fibre texture in absolute terms, but swirled cross-section regions remain and the self-crossing check is still not clean.
experiments.learned: Weighting the direction term harder does not stop crossings. Next: the missing xz/yz normal-grid planes, a seed chosen on a clean region, and the Lasagna normals as an alternative field.

experiments.title: Low deformation regularizer (sym_dirichlet 10 → 2.5) + dense shell at winding 125
experiments.question: If the uniform regularizer is what stops the flow field from stretching into the fat sectors, does relaxing it help?
experiments.technique: loss_weight_sym_dirichlet 2.5 with the dense outer shell active at shell_outer_winding_idx 125, 10k steps on GPU 0.
experiments.result: Worse than baseline on tracks, but the outermost winding now follows the crushed CT boundary within ~0.5 mm in every 30° sector (mean 23.0 vs 23.8 mm; pilot 20.6).
experiments.learned: With the shell active the envelope is right and the interior is wrong: windings are spread incorrectly inside a correct outer boundary. Local spacing supervision (winding model) is the direct remedy, not a uniform stretch or a weaker regularizer. Confounded with the shell; exp-dirlow2 isolates the regularizer.

experiments.title: Winding cache exported to Spiral supervision
experiments.question: Turn the 104 GB native-phase cache into the compact crossing store the fitter reads.
experiments.technique: export_spiral_supervision.py, 4 workers, 106 s; store validated.
experiments.result: 6,902 rays retained (of 7,102), 130,124 crossings, median 16–21 crossings per ray, 1.1 MB store.
experiments.learned: The 104 GB cache reduces to 1 MB of usable supervision; the exporter keeps only each slab's centre ray. Future caches should be sized for rays, not slabs.

experiments.title: First fit with winding-model supervision (+ dense shell at winding 125)
experiments.question: Does local sheet-spacing supervision from the winding model fix the interior distribution of windings?
experiments.technique: dense_spacing_mode winding_model with the exported store (6,900 rays in range, 130k crossings), shell loss weight 1 at winding 125, 10k steps on the 3060 Ti. Both winding-model loss terms active (relative 11.4, density 1.7 at the end).
experiments.result: 0.4213 / 0.0786 — same band as every other shell-active run; no improvement on tracks. w040 render looks like exp-30k's: about half fibre texture, half crossings.
experiments.learned: Either the supervision is too sparse (6,900 rays for 1,000 slices vs ~140k in the documented PHercParis4 run) or the shell pull costs ~4 points regardless. exp-wm2 removes the shell pull (weight 0, shell kept as the required gate) to separate the two.

experiments.title: Patch growing with the community Lasagna normals as the direction field
experiments.question: Is the Fiber-model normal field the limiting input, or would the public Lasagna normals do as well or better?
experiments.technique: Lasagna nx/ny (level 2) converted with make_dirfield_zarr.py, dir: normal, weight 1, xy normal grids, 70 generations, same seed as the Fiber-field run.
experiments.result: 7.1 cm² in 161 s. Best patch so far: the left and centre show the cross-hatched papyrus fibre weave, i.e. on-sheet; the right third still shows laminated crossings. Ink maps (2 seeds × 2 orders) are mottled noise.
experiments.learned: The public Lasagna normals steer the tracer at least as well as the Fiber field. Roughly half the patch is on one sheet; ink needs a clean, flattened sheet, so no letters expected yet. A 150-generation version is running.

experiments.title: Post-hoc snap of exp-30k windings onto the m7 surface prediction (the PHerc. 343 winner's step)
experiments.question: Does moving each vertex onto the nearest predicted sheet turn a half-on-sheet winding into a usable one?
experiments.technique: Nieuwlaar's snap_meshes.py on w020–w119 with the band of the m7 prediction mirrored at level 0: ±15 vox search along normals, jump rejection, Gaussian regularisation. 67 s for 100 windings.
experiments.result: 99.5% of vertices snapped, median move 1.8 vox, only 19% were already within 2 vox. w040 render: modest gain, crossings remain. w070 render: the largest continuous fibre-textured region of any winding so far (~40% of a 3 cm strip) and a clean self-crossing check.
experiments.learned: Snapping fixes small normal offsets but cannot repair regions where the fit crosses between sheets. It does produce the first winding worth the full ink treatment: snapped w070 is flattened, rendered in 66 layers, and in the four-model depth sweep.

experiments.title: Patch growing, Lasagna-normals field, 150 generations
experiments.question: How far does the on-sheet region extend when the Lasagna-guided patch keeps growing?
experiments.technique: As the 70-generation run, 150 generations (796 s).
experiments.result: 35.8 cm² patch; the fibre weave covers roughly half of it (left/centre), laminated crossings on the right. Flattened and rendered in 66 layers; four-model depth sweep queued.
experiments.learned: An on-sheet area of order 15 cm² in one patch is enough for a First Letters search if the ink is there. This and snapped w070 are the two candidates in the ink pipeline.

experiments.title: Winding-model supervision without the shell pull
experiments.question: Separate the winding model's effect from the shell loss that cost every shell-active run ~4 points.
experiments.technique: As exp-wm with loss_weight_shell_outer 0 (shell kept only as the required gate).
experiments.result: 0.4605 / 0.081 — back to the pilot baseline exactly.
experiments.learned: With 6,900 rays the winding-model supervision is neutral, and the shell pull alone explains the ~4-point losses. The fitter route on PHerc0191 is capped near 0.46–0.49 with current inputs; the winner's surface-prediction distance field (old fitter) and the post-hoc snap are what remain to test.

experiments.title: Snapped + flattened w070: 66-layer render and first ink-ensemble depths
experiments.question: With the PHerc. 343 recipe (snap → Lasagna flatten → 66-layer render → four-model ensemble), does the best winding show ink?
experiments.technique: Nieuwlaar's run_depth_sweep.sh / ensemble_maps.py with ink_9um seeds 42/43, dense_native and Hecate 9.6 µm; z-score ensemble on the reading side, blind side for comparison.
experiments.result: The surface layer of the flattened winding shows clean papyrus fibre weave over its whole middle — the best geometry of the campaign. Ink: four-model ensemble at d 0 and ink_9um seed 42 at d +1 (where the 343 letters appeared) are mottled noise on both sides; no rows of letter-sized strokes. The full 31-depth sweep is paused (the 4-core CPU is the bottleneck) after d −2..+2 for the villa models.
experiments.learned: The recipe produces geometry good enough for an ink search. One depth of one winding is not a search: the letters in 343 appeared at d = +1 on one winding of many. Next: geometry triage of all 100 snapped windings, then sweeps on the ones that look like this. Update after the PHerc. 343 positive control: a single model at whole-winding scale misses real ink, so this is not yet evidence of absence; re-check with the full ensemble.

experiments.title: Geometry triage of all snapped windings (flatten + 66-layer render + CT surface layer)
experiments.question: How much of the band is in the same clean on-sheet state as w070?
experiments.technique: For every snapped exp-30k winding from w070 outwards: Lasagna flatten (~7 min GPU), 66-layer render, preview of layer 33 (the surface). Then a fast ink pass (ink_9um seed 42, d +1/0/+2/−1) on each.
experiments.result: w068–w072: papyrus weave over most of each winding (each ~9.3 × 1.9 cm, ~10 cm² after flattening); damage concentrated at the ends. Scale check: flattened renders are 1.02 px/voxel; raw spiral windings were rendered 23–33% compressed (tooling finding #10).
experiments.learned: If this holds across the band, several hundred cm² of searchable sheet exist from one 1,000-slice fit. The ink search, not the geometry, is now the bottleneck.

experiments.title: Positive control: the PHerc. 343 winning segment through our pipeline
experiments.question: Would our ink search see letters where letters are known to be? (If not, our nulls on PHerc. 0191 mean nothing.)
experiments.technique: Erwin Nieuwlaar's published winning mesh, rendered by us in 66 layers straight from the public PHerc. 343 CT; then (a) our fast pass: ink_9um seed 42 at depth +1, whole-segment preview; (b) his full four-model ensemble at depth +1 (ink_9um 42/43, dense_native, Hecate) with his ensemble_maps.py; crops placed on his published letter boxes.
experiments.result: (a) Single model, whole-segment view: letters NOT obvious; only faint blobby structure on the reading side. (b) Four-model ensemble: two rows of bright strokes exactly at the published letter rows; Hecate alone shows them almost as strongly; the two ink_9um seeds averaged show them weakly. Strokes are soft blobs at native zoom, not crisp letters.
experiments.learned: Our pipeline can see prize-grade ink, but only with the ensemble (or Hecate) and a row-scale view. A single model at whole-winding scale would have missed it, so the single-model nulls on w069–w072 are not evidence of absence. The PHerc. 0191 search must use the ensemble.

experiments.title: AWS proof of concept: render + ink on an EC2 GPU next to the data
experiments.question: Can a cloud GPU in us-east-1 run our exact pipeline (render from S3, ink model) and match the home box, quickly and cheaply?
experiments.technique: aws/poc.sh from the Mac: dedicated VPC, on-demand g4dn.2xlarge (Tesla T4, 8 vCPU), Ubuntu 24.04 Deep Learning Base AMI; bootstrap = uv + villa vesuvius env + VC3D Linux AppImage + four ink checkpoints from Hugging Face; job = 66-layer render of the PHerc. 343 control segment straight from the public S3 volume, ink_9um seed 42 at depth +1; fetch; terminate. Spot was tried first but refused in every us-east-1 zone and type that afternoon.
experiments.result: Worked end to end in 7 minutes: bootstrap 2 min, render 43 s (vs 280 s at home), ink map 157 s (vs ~290 s on the CPU-starved home 3060). Output matches the home box: Pearson r 0.99998, max difference 1/255, 97.7% of pixels identical.
experiments.learned: Each cloud T4 does about twice the work of one home GPU, and renders ~6× faster next to the data, for ~$0.75/h on-demand. The ink search can now scale out horizontally; spot capacity for this account is the open question.

experiments.title: Four-model ink ensemble on PHerc. 0191 winding w070 at depths 0 and +1
experiments.question: With the method that passed the PHerc. 343 control, does our best-looking winding show ink?
experiments.technique: Snapped + Lasagna-flattened exp-30k winding w070, 66-layer render; ink_9um seeds 42/43, dense_native and Hecate at depths 0 and +1 (Erwin Nieuwlaar's run_ink.sh / ensemble_maps.py), viewed at row scale on the reading side, checked against the blind side and the CT; scored with the stroke score (next run).
experiments.result: No ink. No rows of strokes at either depth. The only high-scoring patch (depth +1) sits inside a CT crack/void loop at the segment edge and lights up on the blind side too.
experiments.learned: A real null this time (the method sees ink on the control), but only for one ~10 cm² winding at two depths. Next windings w069, w071, w068, w072 are running; damaged CT zones are the main source of false positives.

experiments.title: An automatic stroke score, calibrated on the PHerc. 343 control, to rank windings for review
experiments.question: Can a number computed from the ink maps tell text from no text well enough to decide which windings deserve eyes and the expensive ensemble?
experiments.technique: bin/stroke_score.py: per side (reading vs blind) the ensemble z-score (each model normalised by the reading side's mean/SD, as in ensemble_maps.py), minus a 1.5 mm background; pixels > 2.0 above it; keep 8-connected components of letter-stroke size (0.02–1.5 mm²); ignore a 0.5 mm margin at the segment edge and around CT voids (pinholes filled first). Scores: share of area covered by strokes (reading / blind) and the best 4 mm × 4 mm tile. bin/stroke_rank.sh scores every winding with maps; bin/stroke_watch.sh re-ranks as new maps land.
experiments.result: Control (343, d+1, four models): reading/blind stroke area 12.8×, best reading tile 0.168 vs best blind tile 0.036. PHerc. 0191 w070 (no visible ink): 1.7× (d0) and 2.6× (d+1, from a CT-damage patch), best tile 0.046–0.106. Cheaper model sets still separate the two: three models without Hecate 6.3× vs 1.0–1.1×; ink_9um seed 42 alone 2.2× vs 0.86–0.90×. First ranking of the single-model pass (w066–w074, depths −1..+2): every PHerc. 0191 row 0.83–1.41×, none near the control.
experiments.learned: The ranking can be automated. It is calibrated on one positive segment and one negative winding, so it is a triage aid, not evidence. Two practical wins: the single-model fast pass can pre-rank windings before the slow ensemble, and dropping Hecate (31 min per map at home) may cost little. CT damage (voids, cracks) is the main false-positive source; the top tiles carry a damage fraction.

experiments.title: Four-model ink ensemble on PHerc. 0191 windings w068, w069 and w071 (depths 0, +1)
experiments.question: Do the other clean-weave windings next to w070 show ink with the method that passed the control?
experiments.technique: Same as the w070 run: snapped + Lasagna-flattened exp-30k windings, 66-layer renders, ink_9um 42/43, dense_native and Hecate at depths 0 and +1 on the home box, viewed at row scale (reading side vs blind side vs CT) and scored with the stroke score.
experiments.result: No ink on any of them. Reading-side stroke area 0.0046–0.0066 (control 0.034); w071 has a diffuse brighter cloud at depth 0 next to a long CT crack, with no strokes or rows.
experiments.learned: Four of the five best-geometry windings are now checked with the full ensemble at the two depths where the PHerc. 343 letters sit; none shows text. The search needs more windings (and possibly more depths), which is what the AWS fleet is for.

experiments.title: First real AWS fleet run: four-model ensemble on w073 and w074 on two cloud GPUs
experiments.question: Does the fleet do real work end to end (launch, bootstrap, render from S3, four models, fetch, teardown), how fast is each model on a T4, and do its results match the home box?
experiments.technique: aws/fleet.sh on 2 on-demand g4dn.2xlarge (Tesla T4) in our dedicated VPC; each worker rendered one winding (w073, w074) straight from the public S3 volume and ran ink_9um 42/43, dense_native and Hecate at depths 0 and +1 (Erwin Nieuwlaar's scripts), then his ensemble images; raw maps fetched and stroke-scored on the home box; seed-42 maps compared with the home box's own maps of the same windings.
experiments.result: Worked: both windings done in 1 h 47 min, results fetched, instances terminated; cost $3.28. Both first bootstraps failed at apt-get update (NVIDIA's CUDA package mirror was mid-sync); fixed in the user-data and recovered on the live instances without relaunching. Per depth on a T4: render 48–53 s, ink_9um 90–142 s, dense_native 92–112 s, Hecate ~47 min (two passes). Seed-42 maps match the home box (r 0.99998, max difference 1/255). Ink: none on w073 or w074 by eye; stroke area 0.0055–0.0067, like the other windings.
experiments.learned: Hecate is ~88% of the cost of a four-model winding (~100 min on a T4). A three-model pass without Hecate is ~13 min per winding (~$10 for 59 windings on 10 workers); Hecate can then go only to windings the stroke score flags. Disk is not a bottleneck (everything sits in page cache).

experiments.title: Stroke score v2: rank by absolute stroke area and a 4 cm² window, not by the reading/blind ratio
experiments.question: w073 scored 7.45× reading/blind, far above every other PHerc. 0191 winding. Real, or an artefact of the metric?
experiments.technique: Per-model scores on w073/w074 (AWS) and w068–w071 (home box); raw reading and blind stroke areas; a new First-Letters-scale window (best 2 × 2 cm reading-side stroke share, clamped to the winding height); three-model and four-model sets.
experiments.result: Artefact of the ratio: w073's reading side (0.0066) is like every other winding (0.0046–0.0073); its blind side was unusually quiet (0.0009), and a small denominator inflates the ratio. Absolute metrics separate the control cleanly. Three models: control area 0.0354, reading minus blind +0.030, best window 0.050; PHerc. 0191 ≤ 0.0064, ≤ +0.0021, ≤ 0.017. Four models: control 0.0335 / +0.031 / 0.048; PHerc. 0191 ≤ 0.0073 / ≤ +0.0057 / ≤ 0.023.
experiments.learned: Flag rule now: look at a winding if reading-side stroke area ≥ 0.015, or reading minus blind ≥ 0.010, or its best 4 cm² window ≥ 0.030 (three models) / 0.035 (four). Still calibrated on one positive segment; a triage aid, not evidence.

experiments.title: Ten cloud GPUs, 59 PHerc. 0191 windings: three-model ink pass with automatic stroke scoring
experiments.question: Does any snapped + flattened exp-30k winding outside the central seven show ink, by the stroke score and by eye?
experiments.technique: aws/fleet.sh on 10 on-demand g4dn.2xlarge (Tesla T4): windings w037–w067 and w075–w102, each rendered in 66 layers from the public S3 volume, ink_9um seeds 42/43 and dense_native at depths 0 and +1 (Erwin Nieuwlaar's scripts and ensemble images, Hecate left out for cost), the stroke score computed on each worker; flagged windings checked by eye at row scale and at full resolution against the blind side and the CT.
experiments.result: No ink. All 59 windings done in 1 h 24 min of compute for about $10.70. Reading-side stroke area 0.0029–0.0110 (control 0.035), reading minus blind ≤ +0.0057 (control +0.030). Eight rows on six windings (w083, w090, w100, w101, w102) passed the 4 cm² window line (0.030–0.034, control 0.050); by eye all are diffuse bright mottling, mostly around CT voids or in a brighter zone that recurs at the same position on neighbouring windings, with no strokes and no rows. A shell bug sent each worker only part of its list at first (ssh swallowing the loop input); fixed and recovered on the live workers.
experiments.learned: 66 of the 99 flattened windings in band z 9000–10000 are now checked at depths 0 and +1 (7 with four models, 59 with three); the remaining 33 are running on the home GPUs. A recurring bright zone across windings is the main false-positive source for the window metric; a blind-side check (window ≥ 2× blind) now guards it. The cloud pass costs about $0.18 per winding with three models.

experiments.title: AWS fleet run 3: three-model ink pass on the last 26 windings of band z 9,000–10,000
experiments.question: Do the innermost and outermost windings of the old band (w020–w032, w106–w119), the ones no pass had covered yet, show ink?
experiments.technique: Nine on-demand cloud T4 workers. Each winding rendered in 66 layers from the public S3 volume, ink_9um seeds 42/43 and dense_native at depths 0 and +1 (Erwin Nieuwlaar's scripts), then the stroke score and Scan-Quality-Map on the worker. Flagged rows checked by eye against the blind side and the CT.
experiments.result: No ink. 1 h 10 min, $7.10. Five rows on three windings crossed the look line: w023 and w025 (reading-side stroke area up to 0.018) are core-geometry jumbles where the CT shows folded layers instead of one sheet; w110 (best 4 cm² window 0.038) is speckle. Scan-Quality-Map rates the scan's layer separation at 0.55–0.67 on the inner windings and 0.21–0.36 on the outer ones (it rates the scan, not the mesh). A first attempt stopped before launch, at no cost, because a script was edited while it was running.
experiments.learned: With the home GPUs covering the rest, all 99 flattened windings of the old band are now checked at depths 0 and +1 (7 with four models, 92 with three): no ink. High scores near the core come from folded geometry, not text. And: never edit a script while it is running.

experiments.title: A band chosen by scan clarity: spiral fit and snap of PHerc0191 z 11,200–12,200
experiments.question: Was our old band simply a poor part of the scan? Where is PHerc0191's CT clearest, and does a fit there follow the sheets better?
experiments.technique: Scan-Quality-Map (jcooperkai-sys, MIT) rates how well the papyrus layers separate at each height: our old band scored 0.37–0.40 (scroll median 0.41), the clearest band around z 11,520 scored 0.54. First we checked our depth window against the PHerc. 343 control with air-gap profiles (it matches, so the old nulls were not a depth error). Then the exp-30k recipe (tracks, no shell, 30k steps) on z 11,200–12,200, and Erwin Nieuwlaar's snap of every winding onto the m7 surface prediction.
experiments.result: Our best fit so far with the current spiral fitter: 0.519 of track points on the sheet (old band: 0.490) and 0.138 of tracks fully satisfied (0.102). Snap: 120 windings; on average 90% of each winding's vertices found a predicted sheet, median move 2.1 voxels.
experiments.learned: The old band sat in a below-average part of the scan. The clear band gives the best geometry of the campaign, and it is where PHerc0191 gets its last and deepest look (Phase A).

experiments.title: AWS fleet run 4: the community's PHerc0191 fit (z 11,600–12,400), snapped and inked
experiments.question: Does an independent public fit of PHerc0191, in a different band, show ink with our method?
experiments.technique: rodriguescarson's public fit (10 windings), snapped onto the m7 prediction and Lasagna-flattened on the home box; five cloud T4 workers ran the three-model ink pass at depths 0 and +1, the stroke score and Scan-Quality-Map.
experiments.result: No ink. 30 minutes, $1.50. The ten windings are small fragments, about 0.6 cm² each, in the hollow core of the scroll. Three rows (w008, w009) crossed the look line on edge effects; no 4 cm² window fits on any of them.
experiments.learned: These windings are too small for a First Letters search. Tiny meshes are now on the stroke score's list of known false alarms.

experiments.short: Run 5 stopped; cloud only when it pays
experiments.title: Run 5 stopped before launch: the home GPUs are the default, the cloud only when it pays
experiments.question: Should the 100 windings of the clear band go to a 20-worker cloud run (about $27, about 2 hours)?
experiments.technique: Run 5 was set to start as soon as run 4 finished. Before any instance launched, we stopped it and looked at what the cloud had bought us so far.
experiments.result: Stopped at $0. AWS total for the project: $22.80 over the proof of concept and four fleet runs (table below). Every ink run came back null.
experiments.learned: We were spending money to save time, not to learn something the home box could not. The home GPU box is the default. AWS is for when it is cost-effective, for example to get a fast answer on something promising, not to chase results. Each cloud run needs a fresh go-ahead with the cost stated up front.

experiments.title: Housekeeping: one data layout, data and code dictionaries, 124 GB freed
experiments.question: Can someone new find the inputs and outputs of any step, and can we free disk space without losing results?
experiments.technique: A layout in which every path says scroll, pipeline stage, run and winding, in that order (docs/DATA_LAYOUT.md); a data dictionary (every dataset with format, size, producer and whether it can be deleted) and a code dictionary (every script by pipeline stage). The move ran in a quiet window with a symlink at every old path. Then cleanup tier 1: only regenerable data with no planned use.
experiments.result: Migration done with no broken links; scores re-run through the old paths are identical. Tier 1 freed 124 GB (NVMe 89% → 76%): old-band renders, fibre fields, tracer tests, checkpoints of dropped fit experiments, old QA renders. Meshes, ink maps, scores and fit metrics are kept.
experiments.learned: Bigger deletions wait for decisions: PHerc0191's CT outside the clear band only if Gate A says leave the scroll, the clear-band renders only after Phase A4.

experiments.title: A research plan: fewer, deeper looks, each phase ending at a gate
experiments.question: After three nights of work and four null cloud runs, how do we work from here?
experiments.technique: Ground rules first: home GPUs by default; depth over breadth; every candidate checked against the blind side of the same sheet, the CT and the PHerc. 343 control; the stroke score decides where to look and a person decides what is real; nothing about a possible find is published before the official announcement; every tool, model and dataset is credited.
experiments.result: Four phases. A: finish PHerc0191's clear band (geometry first, pick the best windings by eye, a deep four-model look at depths −2..+3, three models on the rest). B: a pilot on the next scroll (download one band, assemble, fit, snap, judge the geometry). C: the stroke score as a standalone tool, tested on more known text, released before the Oct 31 Progress Prize deadline. D: housekeeping in the gaps. Gate A: strokes anywhere → full depth sweep and close-ups; nothing → stop work on PHerc0191. Gate B: clean geometry → commit to the new scroll; poor → pilot the next one.
experiments.learned: Each phase now ends with a decision we take before the next one starts, instead of covering everything as fast as possible.

experiments.title: Which scroll next? Scan clarity, inputs and prior attempts across the 22 eligible scrolls
experiments.question: Is PHerc0191 still worth the effort, and which eligible scroll should come next?
experiments.technique: For each eligible scroll: the scan protocol, two community clarity measures (Scan-Quality-Map's layer separation and claudepro1515's sheet modulation), the cross-section shape (TAUIL-Abd-Elilah), which inputs our pipeline needs are published (tracks, Lasagna normals, umbilicus, surface prediction), and what others have already tried and reported.
experiments.result: PHerc0191 as a whole is a weak bet: crushed, and mid-table on scan clarity among the scans of its type (4th of 11 on one measure, 9th on the other). Ranked next: PHerc0813 (top three on both measures, a round cross-section, the longest clear stretch, every input published, the same orientation as 0191), then PHerc0358 (clearest on one measure, but folded and with a flipped z direction), then PHerc0175A (clearest of the 8.64 µm scans, but no published Lasagna normals or umbilicus). 0813 over 0358 is a close call.
experiments.learned: Clarity measures are associations across scrolls, not maps of where the ink is. The pipeline that passes the PHerc. 343 control has not been run on 0813, 0358 or 0175A. Finish 0191's clear band first (the data is local and the GPUs are free), then pilot 0813.

experiments.title: stroke-score 0.1: the stroke score as a standalone tool
experiments.question: Can the ranking we use to decide where to look run on anyone's ink maps, without our folder layout?
experiments.technique: Packaged as tools/stroke-score (MIT). Give it a render and any set of ink maps. It builds the ensemble (Erwin Nieuwlaar's normalisation), removes the slow background, keeps bright marks the size of pen strokes, does the same on the blind side of the same sheet, and reports the reading-side stroke area, reading minus blind, the best 4 cm² window, and the best small tiles with review crops (reading | blind | CT). A rank command puts every result in one table and flags rows for a look.
experiments.result: Reproduces our research script exactly (identical scores and top tiles). Validation so far in the table below. Known false alarms, all found by looking at the crops: CT voids and cracks; recurring bright zones at the same place on neighbouring windings; distorted geometry near the core; tiny meshes; and quiet blind sides, which is why it ranks by absolute measures rather than a reading/blind ratio.
experiments.learned: It ranks; it does not prove. A high score means 'look here'. One known-text segment is not enough, so more positives and a measured false-alarm rate come next (Phase C), before the release for the Oct 31 Progress Prize deadline.

experiments.title: Phase A1–A2: all 100 clear-band windings flattened, rendered and triaged; seven picked by eye
experiments.question: Which windings of the clear band show clean papyrus over the largest area?
experiments.technique: Every snapped winding w020–w119: Lasagna flatten on the GPUs, 66-layer render, a CT preview of the surface layer, and montages. Then we went through the montages and picked the windings for the deep look.
experiments.result: 100 windings ready to ink. w070–w074 have the cleanest weave; a damaged, folded zone sits at the same angular position on w060–w074 (the source of the recurring bright zone seen in the old band); the outer windings from w107 on are more laminated. Picks: w070, w071, w072, w073, w074, w087, w089.
experiments.learned: Picking by eye before inking is cheaper than four models on everything, and it puts the expensive models on the best sheet.

experiments.title: Phase A3: four-model ink ensemble at six depths on the seven best clear-band windings
experiments.question: If PHerc0191 has letters where its scan is clearest and our geometry is best, do they show at any depth from −2 to +3?
experiments.technique: ink_9um seeds 42/43, dense_native and Hecate (Erwin Nieuwlaar's run_ink and ensemble scripts) at depths 0/+1, then −1/+2, then −2/+3, on the three home GPUs. Every winding-depth scored with stroke-score 0.1; flags and every pick viewed at row scale, reading side next to blind side next to CT.
experiments.result: No letters. All 168 ink runs finished (none failed) and all 42 winding-depths were scored. The clear band scores higher than the old band: reading-side stroke area 0.0065–0.0115, reading minus blind up to +0.0100, best 4 cm² window up to 0.038 (control: 0.0335, +0.031, 0.048). Two flags, both at depth +2 (table below); depth +3 added none. By eye both come from one cluster of soft, rounded blobs about 1–1.5 mm across, lying along a crack band with voids that the CT shows in the same place, and present at several depths: no strokes, no letter shapes, no rows, and the blind side has the same texture, only dimmer. Judged not writing. Across the seven windings, reading minus blind rises smoothly from depth −2 to +2 and levels off at +3 (chart below), with no peak at one depth.

images.caption: False alarm, w074 at depth +2: reading side | blind side | CT. Soft blobs along a crack band, also faintly on the blind side; no strokes. Judged not writing.

experiments.learned: The strongest PHerc0191 signal yet is a false alarm from a crack band. A difference that grows smoothly through the sheet looks like sheet structure; ink would peak at one depth, as the control does at +1. Gate A gets decided on the whole band (A4), not on seven windings.

experiments.title: Decided: check the whole clear band (A4) and start the PHerc0813 pilot (Phase B)
experiments.question: Seven windings null at six depths: is that enough to leave PHerc0191?
experiments.technique: Gate A talked through with the A3 results, the scroll comparison and the disk plan.
experiments.result: Not yet. A4: a three-model ink check at depths 0 and +1 on the other 93 windings of the clear band, so a null means the whole band is null. Alongside it, the Phase B pilot on PHerc0813: assemble its spiral dataset, fit one band (z 12,000–13,000), snap, and judge the geometry by eye. If A4 is null, PHerc0191 is set aside with its meshes kept; it comes back if a better ink or surface model passes the PHerc. 0343 control.
experiments.learned: A null on seven picked windings is a sample; a null on the whole band is a result.

findings.title: The ink detector is not the problem
findings.text: Calibrated on known text: three legible Greek lines, and the PHerc. 343 control passes with the ensemble. The early PHerc0191 nulls were geometry; since the snap + flatten, the windings have clean papyrus weave, so the nulls after that are real nulls for the windings and depths checked.

findings.title: Positive control passes only with the ensemble
findings.text: On the PHerc. 343 winning segment our four-model ensemble shows the letter rows; ink_9um seed 42 alone at whole-segment scale does not. Searches on 0191 need the ensemble (Hecate is the strongest single model).

findings.title: Minimal-route spiral fits sit on the sheet ~46–49% of the time
findings.text: Satisfaction = within 6 voxels and 0.45 winding of the track's sheet. Weights don't help; 3× steps gives +3 points.

findings.title: The fitted spiral never reaches the outer third
findings.text: Per-sector audit: outermost winding 3–8 mm short of the boundary in the fat sectors; initial spacing fixes the radial extent; stretching hurts the inner tracks.

findings.title: Crushed scroll = same winding count, 2.5× spacing variation by sector
findings.text: 0.13 mm on the flattened sides (ray audit under-counts there) to 0.26 mm at the ends. Needs anisotropic deformation or local spacing supervision.

findings.title: Patch growing needs its normal grids
findings.text: Without normal_grid_path the tracer produces data-independent discs. With them it partly follows sheets.

findings.title: #1 libvolcomp not installed by the VC3D build (fixed, PR #2008)
findings.text: One-line CMake install fix; submitted.

findings.title: #2–#5 image tags, lockfile rewrite, remote-fetch aborts
findings.text: :stable tag missing; uv.lock rewritten by sync; infer and renderer abort on a single transient remote chunk fetch.

findings.title: #6 Shipped track-crossing cache rejected after download
findings.text: Signature uses nanosecond mtime; any download zeroes sub-second mtime. 2.4 GB downloaded for nothing; every run rebuilds.

findings.title: #7 Outer-shell loss silently zero for sparse shells
findings.text: Confidence normalized by an edge spike → 0.22 < 0.25 → no valid samples, no warning. Reproduced outside the fitter.

findings.title: #8 Fiber inference needs lasagna on PYTHONPATH
findings.text: geometry.py imports lasagna.omezarr_pyramid unguarded; the models extra does not ship it.

findings.title: The PHerc. 343 First Letters win (2026-10-08) used our pipeline plus three steps we lacked
findings.text: Spiral fit with the surface-prediction distance field, no shell, 30k steps; post-hoc snap of every vertex onto the nearest predicted sheet (±15 vox); 66-layer render swept over 31 depths through a four-model ink ensemble. All open source; adopted (see notes/prior-art-digest.md).

findings.title: PHerc0191: no ink in any winding checked
findings.text: Band z 9,000–10,000: all 99 flattened windings at depths 0 and +1 (7 four-model, 92 three-model). The community's 10 windings. The seven best clear-band windings at depths −2..+3 with four models. No letters anywhere.

findings.title: Our old band was a below-average part of the scan
findings.text: Scan-Quality-Map: 0.37–0.40 for z 9,000–10,000 against a scroll median of 0.41 and 0.54 for the clearest band, where our fit is also our best (0.519 on-sheet).

findings.title: A crack band can look like a signal
findings.text: The strongest PHerc0191 scores (w073 and w074 at depth +2) came from soft blobs along a CT crack band, present at several depths and faintly on the blind side. Not writing.

findings.title: Next scroll: PHerc0813
findings.text: Top three at 9.362 µm on two clarity measures, round cross-section, the longest clear stretch, every input published, same orientation as PHerc0191. Then PHerc0358, then PHerc0175A.

findings.title: Upstream removed the inputs the winner used (Spiral simplification, 2026-09-23)
findings.text: surf-SDT support and the 'phase' dense-spacing mode were deleted from spiral-fitting three weeks before they won a prize. We run the pre-removal commit in a worktree to reproduce the route.

findings.title: #9 Resident-pool sidecars reused after the source store is rebuilt
findings.text: The fitter silently trained on a stale SDT pool (1 of 1,456 bricks) after the store was rebuilt at the same path.

findings.title: #10 Raw spiral windings render 23–33% compressed
findings.text: Meshes declare a 20-voxel grid but nodes are 26–30 voxels apart; ink models see letters too small unless the winding is flattened first. Mesh areas are understated ~2×.

findings.title: stroke-score 0.1: triage for ink searches (MIT)
findings.text: Ranks windings, depths and 4 cm² windows by stroke-shaped ink on the reading side against the blind side, with review crops. Calibrated on the PHerc. 343 control and 109 null windings; known false alarms documented.

next: Phase A4: three-model ink check (depths 0 and +1) on the other 93 windings of PHerc0191's clear band, on the home GPUs, scored automatically; every flag checked by eye. A null there means the whole band is null.

Phase B pilot on PHerc0813 (band data already downloaded): assemble its spiral dataset, fit one band (z 12,000–13,000), snap, judge the geometry by eye against PHerc0191's clear band. Gate B: clean → commit to 0813; poor → pilot PHerc0358.
If A4 is null: PHerc0191 is set aside with its meshes kept. It comes back if a better ink or surface model passes the PHerc. 0343 control.
Phase C: test stroke-score on more known-text segments, measure its false-alarm rate on our null windings, release before the Oct 31 Progress Prize deadline.
Reader v2 (DomRusso2): test it on the PHerc. 0343 control first; add it to the ensemble only if it shows the letters there.
Progress Prize write-ups for tooling findings #6–#10 (three PRs staged).

pipeline.title: How the pipeline works
pipeline.lede: From an X-ray scan of a rolled-up scroll to a decision about where to look next, in nine steps. Concepts only; each run page has the details.

stages.title: CT scan
stages.text: An X-ray volume of the rolled scroll. Every slice is a cross-section through all of its wound layers.
stages.alt: CT cross-section through PHerc. 0191: crushed and folded layers of papyrus

stages.title: Find the sheet
stages.text: Fit a spiral model of how the papyrus is wound to sheet tracks traced by the community and to predicted surfaces.
stages.alt: Diagram: a squashed spiral following the wound layers, with track points along it

stages.title: Snap
stages.text: Pull the fitted surface onto the papyrus surface a neural network predicted, so it sits on one real sheet.
stages.by: Erwin Nieuwlaar's snap, m7 surface prediction
stages.alt: Diagram: a dashed fitted line pulled down onto the solid predicted surface

stages.title: Flatten
stages.text: Unroll one winding into a flat sheet, so the papyrus, and any writing on it, appear at true size.
stages.alt: A flattened winding: the crossed fibres of the papyrus are visible

stages.title: Render
stages.text: Sample a thin stack of layers just inside and just outside the surface, like slicing the sheet into leaves.
stages.alt: Diagram: thin layers above and below the sheet surface

stages.title: Detect ink
stages.text: Several public ink models each mark where ink might be. Their maps are combined into one ensemble, for the writing side and for the back.
stages.by: ink_9um, dense_native, Hecate; ensemble after Erwin Nieuwlaar
stages.alt: Ensemble ink map of one flattened winding: mottled, no writing

stages.title: Rank
stages.text: The stroke score points to places where stroke-shaped marks show on the writing side but not on the back.
stages.alt: Review crop: writing side, back and CT side by side

stages.title: Look
stages.text: We check every flag by eye against the CT and the back of the sheet. Cracks, voids and folds cause most false alarms.
stages.alt: Diagram: three panels labelled writing side, back and CT

stages.title: Gate
stages.text: Decide: go deeper here, move to the next band, or move to the next scroll. A new band or scroll starts again at step 2.
stages.alt: Diagram: a decision with three ways out: go deeper, next band, next scroll

control.title: Positive control
control.text: Known letters from PHerc. 0343 (Erwin Nieuwlaar's First Letters segment) go through the same render, ink, rank and look steps. The letter rows have to light up there; if they did not, a blank result on our scroll would mean nothing. They do.
control.alt: Ensemble ink map of the PHerc. 0343 control: two rows of bright letter strokes

items.label: Home GPU box
items.text: The default for everything: it costs nothing extra and the data lives there.

items.label: Cloud GPUs
items.text: Short bursts next to the data, only when it is cost-effective, for example to get a fast answer on something promising.
